lines.text: Maps have been essential tools for human navigation for centuries, and the vocabulary surrounding them remains rich and practical even in the digital age. A traditional paper map includes a legend or key explaining its symbols, a scale showing the relationship between map distance and real distance, grid references for pinpointing locations, and contour lines indicating elevation on topographic maps. Compass points — north, south, east, west, and the intermediates (northeast, southwest) — form the fundamental orientation system. Modern digital navigation has introduced its own terminology: GPS (Global Positioning System) uses satellites to determine your coordinates (latitude and longitude). Navigation apps provide turn-by-turn directions, estimated time of arrival (ETA), and real-time traffic updates. They alert you to congestion, roadworks, speed cameras, and suggest alternative routes to avoid delays. Satellite imagery and street view allow you to preview your destination virtually. Maritime navigation uses nautical charts, bearing (compass direction), heading (direction of travel), knots (speed measurement), and port and starboard (left and right of a ship). Aviation adds altitude, flight path, waypoint, and approach. Whether reading an Ordnance Survey map on a British hillside or following a blue dot on your smartphone, spatial literacy — the ability to read, interpret, and communicate geographic information — remains an invaluable skill.

lines.text: The UK's Ordnance Survey (OS) maps are world-famous for their detail and accuracy. 'OS maps' are the gold standard for walkers and hikers. Reading them is taught in schools and is part of the Duke of Edinburgh Award — a national youth achievement programme.

lines.text: British English uses 'sat nav' (satellite navigation); Americans say 'GPS'. The sat nav voice has become a cultural reference — jokes about arguing with the sat nav, ignoring it, or it sending you down a farm track are common British humour.
lines.name: British English uses 'sat nav' (satellite navigation); Americans say 'GPS'. The sat nav voice has become a cultural reference — jokes about arguing with the sat nav, ignoring it, or it sending you down a farm track are common British humour.

lines.text: The British company What3words has divided the entire globe into 3m × 3m squares, each assigned a unique three-word address. Emergency services in the UK now use it for precise location reporting — a modern addition to navigation vocabulary.

lines.text: Britain's maritime heritage means many navigation terms have entered everyday English: 'steer a course', 'plain sailing' (easy), 'all at sea' (confused), 'on an even keel' (stable), 'take the helm' (take charge). These nautical metaphors are used daily.

lines.text: Before smartphones, every Londoner carried an 'A-Z' (pronounced 'A to Zed') — a comprehensive street atlas. 'Checking the A-Z' meant looking up directions. While mostly digital now, 'A-Z' remains a cultural reference for detailed street-level navigation.
